content.intro: This lesson focuses on reliable release and rollback architecture. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Reliable Release and Rollback Architecture matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Release and rollback architecture should promote known artifacts, health-check new releases, retain a previous known-good version, and define who can recover production. Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Release and rollback architecture should promote known artifacts, health-check new releases, retain a previous known-good version, and define who can recover production. Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Release immutability
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Artifact provenance
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

content_blocks.code:
name: Controlled production release
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    concurrency:
      group: production-deploy
      cancel-in-progress: false
    steps:
      - name: Verify release candidate
        run: echo "Verify artifact digest and health checks before promotion"
content_blocks.expected_output: The job is associated with the production environment and a concurrency group; protection rules and the real deployment/rollback commands must be configured separately.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Review environment reviewers and branch restrictions before adding production credentials.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Do not use this sketch to deploy; add an approved known-artifact promotion and tested rollback process first.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to reliable release and rollback architecture. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain reliable release and rollback architecture, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Standardize workflow behavior across teams without hiding important security boundaries.

content.task: Apply reliable release and rollback architecture to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Release and rollback architecture should promote known artifacts, health-check new releases, retain a previous known-good version, and define who can recover production.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Release and rollback architecture should promote known artifacts, health-check new releases, retain a previous known-good version, and define who can recover production. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
